A driver stops his car in time t by gradually increasing the total braking force on the car. The
graph shows the resultant force on the car.

hints: Notice the given force-time graph starts at zero at time $0$ and rises steadily in a straight line to time $t$.
Recall that the gradient of a speed-time graph equals acceleration, and $F = ma$ links resultant force to acceleration.
Since the braking force magnitude grows with time, the downward slope of the speed-time graph must start shallow and become steeper until speed reaches zero at $t$.
walkthrough: Identify the given information: the resultant braking force starts at zero and increases linearly with time up to $t$, while speed must fall from its initial value to zero.
State the governing rule: $F = ma$, so acceleration $a$ is directly proportional to resultant force $F$ for the fixed mass of the car.
Therefore the magnitude of the deceleration is zero at first and then grows steadily larger as time increases.
On a speed-time graph the gradient equals acceleration. Here the gradient must be negative for slowing down, starting near zero and becoming increasingly negative.
That means the speed-time curve is almost flat at $t = 0$ and then curves downward more and more steeply, reaching zero speed at time $t$.
Only the graph that is flat-topped then steepens downward to zero at $t$ matches this. This is option D.

A.explanation: This shows deceleration largest at time zero and then decreasing, which would need a large initial force that falls to zero.

B.explanation: This straight line shows constant gradient and so constant deceleration, which would need a constant resultant braking force.

C.explanation: This S-shape shows the slope first getting steeper then getting shallower, which would need the force to rise then fall.

D.explanation: The slope starts almost horizontal and gets steadily steeper downwards, showing deceleration magnitude increasing as the braking force increases to stop the car at time $t$.
